tagline: The patient spear-fisher of the sand
summary: The largest of all mantis shrimps, this striped ambush hunter lives in a sandy burrow and waits with only its eyes showing. When a fish or shrimp passes, it lunges out and impales it on barbed, spear-like claws — a very different strategy from the hammer-fisted 'smasher' mantis shrimps.

stats.depth: Shallow sandy seabeds; reported to about 145 m
stats.range: Indo-Pacific, from East Africa to Hawaii and the Galápagos

facts.title: Spearer, not smasher
facts.text: Mantis shrimps come in two broad types: 'smashers' roam and hammer hard-shelled prey, while 'spearers' like this one hide in sandy burrows and snatch fast, soft-bodied prey such as fish.

facts.title: Eyes at the doorway
facts.text: Field observations show it hunts mainly at night, hidden in its burrow with just its eyes peeking out, then lunging to grab passing prey.

facts.title: Slower than you'd think
facts.text: Its strikes averaged about 2.3 m/s and lasted about 25 milliseconds — slower than smashers' blows, but similar to other predators that catch evasive prey. Speed, it seems, isn't everything for an ambusher.

facts.title: The biggest mantis shrimp
facts.text: Reaching up to about 40 cm, it is described as the largest mantis shrimp in the world.

facts.title: A couple that shares a home
facts.text: Zebra mantis shrimps are socially monogamous: a male and female share a burrow, and the female cares for the eggs.

references.title: Strike mechanics of an ambush predator: the spearing mantis shrimp (deVries et al. 2012, Journal of Experimental Biology)
